readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: The Forethought
readings.challenge: Read a preface as an argument about how the book should be read.
readings.focus: The color-line, the Veil, and the author’s claim to speak from within.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). The Forethought is the book’s preface. In the printed book each chapter opens with a verse epigraph and a bar of music from the Sorrow Songs, the spirituals of the enslaved; the music is not reproduced here. “Gentle Reader” is an old courteous address to the reader, and “bone of the bone and flesh of the flesh” echoes Genesis 2:23.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: The Forethought, complete; opens “HEREIN lie buried many things which if read with patience may show the strange meaning of…”; closes “ATLANTA, GA., Feb. 1, 1903.”.

questions.prompt: Du Bois addresses a “Gentle Reader” and asks to be received “in all charity.” Whom does he seem to imagine reading, and what does he ask of that reader?
facilitatorNotes: Chiefly a white reader outside the Veil: he says he has left “the white world” and raised the Veil “that you may view faintly” what lies within. He asks for patience and for study “with me,” and excuses his mistakes by his “faith and passion.” The humility is also a demand to be read seriously. Some readers will point out that the closing sentence speaks to Black readers too.
evidence: Leaving, then, the white world, I have stepped within the Veil, raising it that you may view faintly its deeper recesses
studying my words with me

questions.prompt: Use the third and fourth paragraphs to map the book. Where does it move from the world outside the Veil to the world within, and why might that order matter?
facilitatorNotes: It moves from Emancipation and its aftermath, leadership, the two worlds, and the training of men, through the Black peasantry and the relations of “master and man,” to religion, sorrow, “greater souls,” a story, and song. The order goes from history and policy a white reader might recognise toward the inner life, so the book itself raises the Veil step by step. Others describe the same order as a move from argument to art.
evidence: the spiritual world in which ten thousand thousand Americans live and strive
the meaning of its religion, the passion of its human sorrow, and the struggle of its greater souls

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois set a bar of the Sorrow Songs before each chapter, and what claim does he make for that music?
facilitatorNotes: He calls it “the only American music” that came from Black souls in the past, a large claim that the most original American art was made by the enslaved. Setting it beside epigraphs from Byron, Schiller and Whittier puts two traditions side by side. A reader who cannot read music meets a sign of something the reader cannot fully enter, which may be part of the point.
evidence: some echo of haunting melody from the only American music which welled up from black souls in the dark past

questions.prompt: The Forethought ends with a question: “need I add …?” Why end on this claim, and how does it change the authority of the book?
facilitatorNotes: He claims kinship, not only knowledge: he writes as a member of the people he describes, not as an outside observer, however learned. Framing it as a question suggests the point should be obvious. Some readers connect it with the double-consciousness of the book’s first chapter: he writes from within the Veil to readers outside it.
evidence: I who speak here am bone of the bone and flesh of the flesh of them that live within the Veil

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: freedom, the ballot, and book-learning (Chapter I)
readings.challenge: Trace a history told as a series of ideals, each replacing the last.
readings.focus: Emancipation as a promised land, and the disappointments that followed it.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter I has introduced the Veil and double-consciousness, the sense of seeing oneself through the eyes of a contemptuous world. The first verse is from a spiritual of Emancipation; the second is Macbeth’s cry to the ghost of Banquo, whom he has had murdered, at his banquet. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) forbade denying the vote on account of race; “the revolution of 1876” is the end of Reconstruction, when federal protection was withdrawn from the South.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage mentions the terror of the Ku-Klux Klan.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Of Our Spiritual Strivings,” from “Away back in the days of bondage” to the ideal of “book-learning”; opens “Away back in the days of bondage they thought to see in one divine event the end of all…”; closes “…and law, steep and rugged, but straight, leading to heights high enough to overlook life.”.

questions.prompt: Name the three ideals that, in Du Bois’s account, led the freed people after Emancipation. What became of each?
facilitatorNotes: Freedom itself, “the key to a promised land,” which came “like a dream” and left disappointment; the ballot, seen after the Fifteenth Amendment as the chief means to liberty, until 1876 left the “half-free serf weary”; and “book-learning,” which “seemed” the mountain path to Canaan. The word “seemed” warns that this ideal too will prove incomplete on its own, as the chapter goes on to argue.
evidence: Emancipation was the key to a promised land
he now regarded as the chief means of gaining and perfecting the liberty
It was the ideal of "book-learning"

questions.prompt: Why quote Macbeth’s words to Banquo’s ghost? Who or what is the “swarthy spectre” at the Nation’s feast?
facilitatorNotes: The spectre is the unsolved race problem, and the people the nation treats as a problem, returning to a nation celebrating forty years of progress. Banquo is the victim of Macbeth’s own crime, so the allusion implies guilt, as the next sentence says: “The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins.” Some readers hear bitter irony in casting Black Americans as a ghost at a feast rather than as guests.
evidence: the swarthy spectre sits in its accustomed seat at the Nation's feast
The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins

questions.prompt: Find the language of the Exodus in the passage (Israelites, promised land, pillar of fire, Canaan). What does it claim about the freed people’s history?
facilitatorNotes: It makes Emancipation an Exodus and the freed people a people on a sacred journey, borrowing the language of the spirituals themselves. The “forty years” since freedom recall Israel’s forty years in the wilderness: the journey is long and unfinished. It also lends a political history the dignity of scripture.
evidence: another pillar of fire by night after a clouded day
Here at last seemed to have been discovered the mountain path to Canaan

questions.prompt: Du Bois says the disappointment was bitter “because the unattained ideal was unbounded save by the simple ignorance of a lowly people.” Is he blaming the freed people for hoping too much?
facilitatorNotes: Not mainly. He explains the bitterness by the size of the hope, held by people who could not yet know how a hostile nation would limit it, and he names the real obstacles: war, the Klan, lying carpet-baggers, contradictory advice. Phrases like “headless host” and “bewildered serf” can still sound condescending, and students may weigh that tone against his sympathy.
evidence: a disappointment all the more bitter because the unattained ideal was unbounded save by the simple ignorance of a lowly people
The holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: Sherman’s march and the making of a Bureau (Chapter II)
readings.challenge: Follow a legislative history and notice where the historian’s judgment shows through.
readings.focus: How a wartime improvisation became the Freedmen’s Bureau.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter II is Du Bois’s history of the Freedmen’s Bureau (1865–1872), the federal agency created to aid the formerly enslaved. It has described how fugitives poured into Union lines during the Civil War and how officers improvised camps, wages and schools. General William T. Sherman’s army marched through Georgia to Savannah in late 1864; his Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) set aside coastal land for freed families. Charles Sumner was an antislavery senator from Massachusetts.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Of the Dawn of Freedom,” from Sherman’s march to the act of 1865; opens “Three characteristic things one might have seen in Sherman's raid through Georgia, which…”; closes “…the hands of the Bureau for eventual lease and sale to ex-slaves in forty-acre parcels.”.

questions.prompt: Du Bois names three “characteristic things” in Sherman’s march. Why does the third speak to him “with so deep a meaning,” and how does he make it vivid?
facilitatorNotes: The fugitives following the army embody what the war was really about, which neither the conquering soldiers nor the defenders of the Lost Cause admit. “Like remorse” makes them the nation’s conscience trailing its army; the verbs “trudged and writhed and surged” give them a force that orders and broken bridges cannot stop. Words like “cloud” and “horde” may seem to blur individuals, though they also show how the army saw them.
evidence: that dark human cloud that clung like remorse on the rear of those swift columns
In vain were they ordered back, in vain were bridges hewn from beneath their feet

questions.prompt: What was “the characteristic military remedy,” and why might Du Bois call it characteristic?
facilitatorNotes: Field Order No. 15, reserving the Sea Islands and abandoned rice-fields for freed families. It is characteristic because an army settles a vast social question by a single order: quick and sweeping, but made “by act of war” and so legally uncertain once the war ended. Some readers find a note of admiration for its decisiveness beside Congress’s delays.
evidence: There too came the characteristic military remedy
are reserved and set apart for the settlement of Negroes now made free by act of war

questions.prompt: Trace the steps from Representative Eliot’s bill to the act of 1865. Where does Du Bois’s wording reveal his judgment of the process?
facilitatorNotes: A bill “never reported,” “half-hearted steps,” regulations suspended for “public policy” (his quotation marks signal doubt), debates that “wandered,” a bill “whirled through” at the session’s end, and “a hasty bit of legislation.” He is not simply hostile: he calls Fessenden’s regulations “excellent.”
evidence: Some half-hearted steps were taken
This last compromise was a hasty bit of legislation, vague and uncertain in outline.

questions.prompt: Look at the terms of the act of 1865: its length of life, its staff, and its land. What problems do they lead you to predict?
facilitatorNotes: It was to last only through the war and one year after, with no more than ten clerks for the whole work, and it depended on abandoned land that might be reclaimed. A reader can predict a short-lived, under-staffed agency making promises of land it could not keep. Students may predict other troubles; the next part of the chapter tests them.
evidence: to continue during the present War of Rebellion, and for one year thereafter
with an office force not exceeding ten clerks
for eventual lease and sale to ex-slaves in forty-acre parcels

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: two figures of a woful day (Chapter II)
readings.challenge: Move from constitutional argument to allegory, and ask why the historian needs both.
readings.focus: The Bureau’s powers, the forces against it, and the two figures who stand for the age.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter II has told how the Freedmen’s Bureau was created in 1865 for one year after the war and how it began its work. President Andrew Johnson, Lincoln’s successor, opposed it. The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery, the Fourteenth (1868) made the freed people citizens, and the Fifteenth (1870) protected their vote. Carpet-baggers were Northerners who went South after the war, often for office or profit.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The last paragraph alludes to the rape of an enslaved woman by her enslaver and the killing of her son by night riders, and quotes their racial slur. Du Bois also concedes that some slavery had “something of kindliness,” a claim the questions examine.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Of the Dawn of Freedom,” from the act of 1866 to the two figures of the Reconstruction South; opens “Evidently, Congress must soon legislate again on the hastily organized Bureau, which had…”; closes “…hating, they went to their long home, and, hating, their children's children live to-day.”.

questions.prompt: Du Bois calls both arguments over the 1866 bill “unanswered, and indeed unanswerable.” What were they, and why does he not simply declare one right?
facilitatorNotes: The Bureau’s extraordinary powers threatened the civil rights of all citizens; yet the government had to do what “manifestly must be done,” or abandoning the freed people meant their re-enslavement. Holding both shows a real dilemma for a democracy using emergency power, and the historian’s fairness. Many readers will still see where his sympathy lies.
evidence: These two arguments were unanswered, and indeed unanswerable
present abandonment of the freedmen meant their practical re-enslavement

questions.prompt: “The Freedmen’s Bureau became a full-fledged government of men.” What powers does Du Bois list, and why does he then insist on “the drift of things in the later sixties”?
facilitatorNotes: It made, enforced and interpreted laws, taxed, punished crime and used military force. He turns to the setting because judgment needs it: Lincoln dead, Johnson fighting Congress, guerrilla raids against the freed people, poverty everywhere. Any such agency was “in large part foredoomed.” A skeptic may call this an excuse; Du Bois goes on to criticise the Bureau’s agents himself.
evidence: It made laws, executed them and interpreted them
the work of any instrument of social regeneration was in large part foredoomed to failure

questions.prompt: Du Bois says the freed slave came from “not the worst slavery in the world.” Why might he make this concession, and does the rest of the paragraph take it back?
facilitatorNotes: It may be meant to seem fair to white readers, or it may reflect comparisons common in his time. The sentence turns at “but withal slavery,” which “classed the black man and the ox together,” and the next paragraph’s image of the mother leaves no comfort. Students may judge the concession a tactic or a real blind spot; both readings can be argued from the text.
evidence: not the worst slavery in the world, not a slavery that made all life unbearable
but withal slavery, which, so far as human aspiration and desert were concerned, classed the black man and the ox together

questions.prompt: Describe the two figures in the final paragraph. What does each represent, and what does Du Bois mean by “hating, their children’s children live to-day”?
facilitatorNotes: The ruined old planter stands for the white South that tolerated slavery; the Black mother who served, nursed, was forced by her master, and saw her son, his child, killed by night riders stands for the enslaved and freed. Their hands never meet, and the hatred passes to the next generations, into 1903. Some read the pair as balanced tragedy; others notice that the mother’s suffering is far greater and that the planter is father to the murdered son.
evidence: no man clasped the hands of these two passing figures of the present-past
and, hating, their children's children live to-day

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: the legacy of the Freedmen’s Bureau (Chapter II, end)
readings.challenge: Weigh an imagined alternative history against the record of what happened.
readings.focus: What the Bureau might have been, why it died, and what it left.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter II has traced the Freedmen’s Bureau (1865–1872) through its schools, courts and Freedmen’s Bank, the bank’s collapse, and the decision to give Black men the vote. Peons are laborers bound by debt; social settlements were neighborhood houses where reformers lived among the poor. “The King’s Highway” is a biblical phrase for a main road.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Of the Dawn of Freedom,” the last four paragraphs; opens “Had political exigencies been less pressing, the opposition to government guardianship of…”; closes “…duty and the deed. The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.”.

questions.prompt: What “far better policy” does the “social seer” imagine? Which parts of it did the Bureau attempt, and which never existed?
facilitatorNotes: A permanent Bureau, national schools, a supervised labor office, impartial protection in the regular courts, savings-banks, land and building associations and settlements, together “a great school of prospective citizenship.” The Bureau had schools, its own courts and a bank, but only temporarily; permanence and impartial regular courts never came. Students may ask whether such guardianship could ever have won consent.
evidence: a permanent Freedmen's Bureau, with a national system of Negro schools
a great school of prospective citizenship

questions.prompt: “So the Freedmen’s Bureau died, and its child was the Fifteenth Amendment.” What does the metaphor imply about the Bureau and the vote?
facilitatorNotes: The vote replaced the Bureau’s protection: the nation treated suffrage as “a final answer” and let its guardian die. The child is an heir but also an orphan, left without protection. Du Bois blames the Bureau too, for its agents’ political ambition. Some readers take the image as honoring the Amendment as the Bureau’s greatest achievement.
evidence: It came to regard its work as merely temporary, and Negro suffrage as a final answer to all present perplexities.
So the Freedmen's Bureau died, and its child was the Fifteenth Amendment.

questions.prompt: “The Negro is not free.” What evidence does Du Bois give for 1903, and how does he explain crime?
facilitatorNotes: Workers bound to plantations, peonage, a “segregated servile caste,” unequal courts, and taxation without representation, the Revolution’s own slogan. Crime is the result that “in nature must have been,” which reverses the common claim that crime proved Black inferiority. A reader may want more evidence than assertion here, though his readers knew these conditions.
evidence: Taxation without representation is the rule of their political life.
And the result of all this is, and in nature must have been, lawlessness and crime.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends with a prose poem and repeats the sentence that opened it. How does the figure “veiled and bowed” sum up the chapter, and why repeat the color-line sentence?
facilitatorNotes: Amid a sunny, fruitful land a bowed, veiled figure sits by the road, and travellers hurry past: the nation avoiding what it owes. “Now behold a century new for the duty and the deed” turns history into a call to act. Repeating the opening sentence makes the whole history of the Bureau evidence for the chapter’s thesis.
evidence: there in the King's Highway sat and sits a figure veiled and bowed, by which the traveller's footsteps hasten as they go
now behold a century new for the duty and the deed

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: a dynasty of leaders (Chapter III)
readings.challenge: Test a three-part scheme against the history it organizes.
readings.focus: Revolt, adjustment and self-development in a century and a half of Black leadership.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), head of Tuskegee Institute, urged Black Southerners to put industrial training and property ahead of agitation for civil and political rights, most famously at the Atlanta Exposition of 1895. Chapter III has praised his work and argued that honest criticism of leaders is “the soul of democracy.” Du Bois names many figures briefly: the Maroons were communities of escaped slaves; Cato led the Stono rebellion in South Carolina (1739); “Phyllis” is the poet Phillis Wheatley; Crispus Attucks died in the Boston Massacre (1770); Gabriel, Denmark Vesey and Nat Turner led or planned slave revolts; David Walker’s Appeal (1829) urged the enslaved to resist; Frederick Douglass was the great abolitionist. The “Revolution of 1876” is the end of Reconstruction.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage recalls slave revolts and uses the period term “mulatto.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,” from the three attitudes of an imprisoned group to Washington’s rise; opens “Now in the past the American Negro has had instructive experience in the choosing of…”; closes “…began to recognize Mr. Washington's leadership; and the voice of criticism was hushed.”.

questions.prompt: What three attitudes may an “imprisoned group” take? Sort some of the leaders Du Bois names before 1830 among them.
facilitatorNotes: Revolt and revenge (the Maroons, Cato, Gabriel, Vesey, Turner); adjustment and assimilation (Wheatley, Attucks, Banneker, the Cuffes, in the late eighteenth century); and self-development (the African Church). Some figures resist sorting: the African Church withdrew from white churches but built something lasting, and students may argue where Walker belongs.
evidence: a feeling of revolt and revenge; an attempt to adjust all thought and action to the will of the greater group; or, finally, a determined effort at self-realization and self-development despite environing opinion

questions.prompt: What did the free Black leaders of the North ask for around 1830, and why did “the trend of the times” refuse them?
facilitatorNotes: To be recognised as freemen, “people of color,” on the same terms as other men, while acknowledging that others were enslaved. The nation lumped them with “all the despised blacks,” took away their votes, and offered only colonization, which they refused, so they turned to Abolition. Du Bois lists, without comment, “Du Bois of New Haven,” probably his own grandfather Alexander, so the family history is part of the dynasty.
evidence: as "people of color," not as "Negroes."
considered them as one with all the despised blacks

questions.prompt: How was Booker T. Washington a new kind of leader, according to the last paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: Earlier leaders rose “by the silent suffrage of their fellows” and led their own people; Washington is “the leader not of one race but of two,” a compromiser recognised first by national opinion and by a North investing in the South. His authority came largely from outside. A defender could answer that a leader trusted by both races was what the moment needed.
evidence: Nearly all the former ones had become leaders by the silent suffrage of their fellows
Booker T. Washington arose as essentially the leader not of one race but of two

questions.prompt: Du Bois calls the succession of leaders “a peculiar dynasty.” Where does Washington stand in it, and where would Du Bois place himself?
facilitatorNotes: Washington revives the old attitude of adjustment, now with civil and political rights given up for economic chances. Du Bois aligns himself with Douglass’s “ultimate assimilation through self-assertion, and on no other terms,” and with the third attitude of self-development “despite environing opinion.” Students may argue that the scheme was built to make that conclusion look inevitable.
evidence: Douglass, in his old age, still bravely stood for the ideals of his early manhood,--ultimate assimilation through self-assertion, and on no other terms.

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: a duty stern and delicate (Chapter III, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a critique that separates praise from opposition with care.
readings.focus: Judging the South with discrimination, Washington’s three half-truths, and where the burden belongs.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter III has argued that Washington’s program asks Black Americans to give up political power, civil rights and higher education for the time being, and that the educated cannot stay silent. Governor Charles Aycock of North Carolina championed schools for both races, though he had also campaigned for disfranchisement; Senator John T. Morgan of Alabama urged removing Black Americans from the country; Thomas Nelson Page wrote fiction glorifying the plantation; Senator Ben Tillman of South Carolina defended lynching. Joshua led Israel into Canaan after Moses.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage refers to lynching.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,” the last six paragraphs; opens “First, it is the duty of black men to judge the South discriminatingly. The present…”; closes “…unalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois insist that “the South” is not one thing? Which white Southern attitudes does he distinguish, and what does each lead to?
facilitatorNotes: The ignorant hate (and lynch), workingmen fear competition, money-makers want cheap labor (semi-slavery), some of the educated fear Black progress (disfranchisement, deportation), and some “sons of the masters” help. Distinguishing makes precise criticism possible: praise Aycock and denounce Tillman “in the same breath.” Students may ask whether the friendly “sons of the masters” are drawn too generously.
evidence: the ignorant Southerner hates the Negro, the workingmen fear his competition, the money-makers wish to use him as a laborer
to inveigh indiscriminately against "the South" is unjust

questions.prompt: State Washington’s three propositions as Du Bois summarizes them, and the “supplementary truths” he sets beside them. Why call them half-truths rather than lies?
facilitatorNotes: That the South is justified by Black “degradation” (but slavery and prejudice are causes); that wrong past education explains slow progress (but common and industrial schools needed teachers from higher institutions); that the future depends on Black effort (but it needs the encouragement of the “richer and wiser” group). Each contains truth and leaves out the cause that would place responsibility elsewhere. Students may test whether the summary is fair, since Du Bois also credits Washington’s stand against lynching.
evidence: Each of these propositions is a dangerous half-truth.
slavery and race-prejudice are potent if not sufficient causes of the Negro's position

questions.prompt: “The burden belongs to the nation.” How does Du Bois widen responsibility to the North, and what is the force of his question about “nine millions of men”?
facilitatorNotes: Washington’s teaching lets whites stand aside as “spectators”; the North is “co-partner in guilt” and cannot buy its conscience clear with gifts and investment. The final question makes injustice a danger to the nation’s own moral survival, not only to its victims. Readers can discuss whether “murder” is literal (lynching) or a figure for slow destruction, or both.
evidence: The North--her co-partner in guilt--cannot salve her conscience by plastering it with gold.
can the moral fibre of this country survive the slow throttling and murder of nine millions of men?

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, what will Du Bois support in Washington’s program and what will he oppose? Why end with the Declaration of Independence?
facilitatorNotes: He will support thrift, patience and industrial training, holding up Washington’s hands as Aaron and Hur held up Moses’; he will oppose apology for injustice, neglect of the vote, acceptance of caste, and opposition to higher training. Ending with the Declaration claims the nation’s founding creed, which “the sons of the Fathers would fain forget”: the heirs, not the excluded, have abandoned it. Some hear the praise of “this Joshua” as sincere, others as strategic.
evidence: we must hold up his hands and strive with him
clinging unwaveringly to those great words which the sons of the Fathers would fain forget

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: three streams of thought (Chapter VI, part 1)
readings.challenge: Untangle three “thoughts” and the “afterthought” that shadows each.
readings.focus: A world hungry for labor, the older South, and the self-doubt of the oppressed.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). The chapter’s epigraph comes from Edward FitzGerald’s translation of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám. In 1619 the first enslaved Africans in English North America were brought to Virginia, near Jamestown. A tertium quid is a “third thing,” neither one nor the other; the Zeitgeist is the spirit of the age. Du Bois wrote as the United States and the European powers were seizing colonies in Asia and Africa.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Du Bois voices racist beliefs in order to expose them (the Negro as “a clownish, simple creature”), and himself calls some men “black, backward, and ungraceful.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Of the Training of Black Men,” from the epigraph to the call for Education; opens “Why, if the Soul can fling the Dust aside, And naked on the Air of Heaven ride, Were't…”; closes “…us to the wail of prisoned souls within the Veil, and the mounting fury of shackled men.”.

questions.prompt: Name the three “streams of thinking.” Whose thought is each, and what “afterthought” lurks behind it?
facilitatorNotes: The thought of the wider world, that trade unites all men, behind which lurks “force and dominion”; the older South’s belief that the Negro is a tertium quid between men and cattle, behind which lurks the fear that some might become men and must be kept down; and Black Americans’ own cry for opportunity, behind which lurks the doubt that the world may be right. The repeated pattern shows each hope with its shadow.
evidence: behind this thought lurks the afterthought of force and dominion
suppose, after all, the World is right and we are less than men?

questions.prompt: Why does the third afterthought, the self-doubt of “men who are black and whitened,” matter to an essay about education? How does the epigraph bear on it?
facilitatorNotes: Oppression enters the mind of the oppressed, a form of the double-consciousness of Chapter I; so education must reach the soul, not only teach a trade. The epigraph asks why a soul that could ride the air should stay “crippled” in clay, which anticipates Du Bois’s claim that training must free the spirit. Some read “whitened” as mixed ancestry, others as taught to see through white eyes.
evidence: the confused, half-conscious mutter of men who are black and whitened
a shriek in the night for the freedom of men who themselves are not yet sure of their right to demand it

questions.prompt: In the fifth and sixth paragraphs Du Bois argues partly from self-interest. What dangers does he warn of, and who is the “we” here?
facilitatorNotes: “We” is the nation, spoken to largely as white readers: refuse to develop these workers and risk poverty; exploit them and risk “national decadence”; scorn their ambition and reap crime. He even borrows employers’ language, “a stalwart laboring force.” Students may judge this a shrewd strategy for persuading a hostile audience or an uncomfortable concession.
evidence: Only that saner selfishness, which Education teaches men, can find the rights of all in the whirl of work.
a stalwart laboring force, suited to the semi-tropics

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois propose to meet color prejudice, and what is surprising in his wish to “encourage the prejudices that bulwark society”?
facilitatorNotes: Not by ridicule, attack or law alone, but by “the breadth and broadening of human reason,” culture itself. He separates prejudices that, as he sees it, protect social order from those that deafen men to “the wail of prisoned souls.” Modern readers may find any defence of prejudice startling; it may be a concession to readers who feared upheaval, or a sign of his own respect for custom.
evidence: They can be met in but one way,--by the breadth and broadening of human reason, by catholicity of taste and culture.
such training as will give us poise to encourage the prejudices that bulwark society

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: the Gates of Toil (Chapter VI, part 2)
readings.challenge: Follow a short history of schooling to the question it is built to raise.
readings.focus: Four decades of Black education in the South, and the limits of the industrial school.
readings.context: Recap: Du Bois has set out three streams of thought about Black Americans (a world hungry for labor, an older South that saw them as less than men, and their own self-doubt) and found that all agree on Education as the cure. Dr. Johnson is Samuel Johnson, the eighteenth-century English critic. Normal schools trained teachers. “Is not life more than meat, and the body than raiment?” comes from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:25). “The crazy imperialism of the day” refers to the colonial wars of the 1890s, among them the United States’ war in the Philippines.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Of the Training of Black Men,” from the truism of Education to “Is not life more than meat?”; opens “But when we have vaguely said that Education will set this tangle straight, what have we…”; closes “…than bread-winning, is the privilege of white men and the danger and delusion of black.”.

questions.prompt: Du Bois divides the years since the Civil War into four periods. Name them and the problem each faced.
facilitatorNotes: To 1876, groping and temporary relief (army, mission and Bureau schools); the next ten years, building school systems with normal schools and colleges; from about 1885 to 1895, the South’s industrial revolution, with weak colleges, poor common schools, hardening prejudice and competition from poor whites; and from 1895, the industrial school’s full recognition. Each answer creates the next problem.
evidence: From the close of the war until 1876, was the period of uncertain groping and temporary relief.
The industrial school springing to notice in this decade, but coming to full recognition in the decade beginning with 1895

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois praise the industrial school, and how does the image of the gates turn praise into a limit?
facilitatorNotes: He calls it “an answer of singular wisdom and timeliness” that gave handiwork dignity. Then “before the Temple of Knowledge swing the Gates of Toil,” and “Yet after all they are but gates”: work is the entrance, not the destination. One image both honors Washington’s program and puts it in its place.
evidence: before the Temple of Knowledge swing the Gates of Toil
Yet after all they are but gates

questions.prompt: What “sinister signs” does Du Bois see in recent educational movements? How do they connect with “the crazy imperialism of the day”?
facilitatorNotes: Treating people as “material resources” trained for “future dividends,” with race prejudice welcomed as a way to keep workers in their “places.” Imperialism treats colonized peoples the same way, as labor; the first part of the chapter spoke of making “brown men to delve.” Du Bois links Southern school policy to a world-wide pattern.
evidence: to regard human beings as among the material resources of a land to be trained with an eye single to future dividends
Race-prejudices, which keep brown and black men in their "places," we are coming to regard as useful allies

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois ask his question “gently, but in all sincerity,” and in the words of the Gospel? What does the quotation claim education is for?
facilitatorNotes: The gentle tone avoids a direct attack on a popular leader, and the Gospel speaks to his readers’ faith: life is more than bread, education more than bread-winning, “culture and character.” The last sentence names what is at stake, an education reserved as “the privilege of white men.” Some find the “gently” ironic, given how sharply the paragraph ends.
evidence: to ask gently, but in all sincerity, the ever-recurring query of the ages
is the privilege of white men and the danger and delusion of black

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: a boulder of New England granite (Chapter VI)
readings.challenge: Notice how an argument from evidence makes room for a memorial.
readings.focus: The case against Black colleges, and Du Bois’s answer from history and numbers.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter VI has argued that industrial schools are only “gates” to education and shown that Black schooling in the South began with colleges and normal schools, which trained the teachers for the common schools. Atlanta University, where Du Bois taught, and Fisk, Howard and the others were founded after the war, largely by Northern missionary teachers. “A priori” means before looking at the evidence. Commissioner Harris was William T. Harris, the United States Commissioner of Education.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Du Bois quotes a Southern newspaper’s contempt for Black students as learning “in a parrot-like way.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Of the Training of Black Men,” from the charge that higher training was “forced” to the count of graduates; opens “It can thus be seen that the work of education in the South began with higher…”; closes “…must be increased to five times its present average" to equal the average of the land.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Southern editorial claim, and which four questions does Du Bois say “cannot be evaded”? On what terms will he answer them?
facilitatorNotes: That classical training failed, students learning “in a parrot-like way.” The questions: are enough students ready, are too many forced, does it make them dissatisfied, and do graduates succeed? He grants the questions but insists on evidence, since most Americans answer them “a priori.” Granting fair questions makes his answer more persuasive.
evidence: most Americans answer all queries regarding the Negro a priori
the least that human courtesy can do is to listen to evidence

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois interrupt his survey of colleges with the inscription on a grave? What does the inscription itself stress?
facilitatorNotes: The boulder placed by graduates for a former teacher is evidence of a bond that statistics cannot show, and “as I write” places Du Bois on that campus. The inscription stresses friendship, an unselfish life, and blessing passed to “their children’s children”: education as an inheritance. A skeptic may call it sentiment rather than evidence; Du Bois seems to think the bond is the evidence.
evidence: Through the shining trees that whisper before me as I write
AND OF THE UNSELFISH LIFE HE

questions.prompt: “Not alms, but a friend; not cash, but character.” What was the gift of New England, and why does Du Bois call the teachers’ crusade “that finest thing in American history”?
facilitatorNotes: Teachers who lived and worked with their students, making the colleges “social settlements”: “the contact of living souls.” It was untainted by greed in an age of greed, the opposite of education for dividends. He adds that such love can now come only from “their own kindred and race,” which is the case for Black college graduates as teachers. Some readers will notice the paternalism in “their favored children.”
evidence: This was the gift of New England to the freed Negro: not alms, but a friend; not cash, but character.
for it was the contact of living souls

questions.prompt: How does the figure of “about two thousand” graduates answer one of the editorial’s questions, and what does Commissioner Harris’s figure add?
facilitatorNotes: Two thousand among millions cannot be “too large a proportion”; Harris says Black enrollment in higher and secondary schooling would have to grow fivefold to equal the national average. Higher training is under-supplied, not overdone. Numbers do not answer the question of quality, which Du Bois takes up next.
evidence: The number in itself is enough to put at rest the argument that too large a proportion of Negroes are receiving higher training.
it must be increased to five times its present average

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: what the graduates did (Chapter VI)
readings.challenge: Judge a social scientist’s evidence, including his own testimony.
readings.focus: What college-trained Black men and women did with their training, and what the South will need of them.
readings.context: Recap: answering a Southern editorial that called Black college training a waste, Du Bois has described the colleges founded by New England teachers after the war and counted about two thousand graduates. The Atlanta University Conferences, which Du Bois directed, published yearly studies of Black American life; the 1900 study was The College-Bred Negro. Tuskegee Institute was Booker T. Washington’s school, and Hampton Institute, where Washington studied, was its model.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Du Bois speaks of “a certain unpleasant rawness and gaucherie” in a people a generation from slavery.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Of the Training of Black Men,” from the record of the graduates to the place of the college in the South; opens “Fifty years ago the ability of Negro students in any appreciable numbers to master a…”; closes “…strange to relate, largely silent or antagonistic to the higher education of the Negro.”.

questions.prompt: How did the Atlanta Conference study the graduates, and how does Du Bois handle the weaknesses of his evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Questionnaires answered by nearly two-thirds of the living graduates, checked against the colleges’ reports. He admits the difficulties of reaching people, trusting testimony and defining success, and grants that many of the missing third may have failed. He then adds personal knowledge of more than a thousand graduates. Students can debate whether that testimony strengthens the case or weakens its objectivity.
evidence: It is of course extremely difficult to collect satisfactory data on such a point
Granting even that a considerable proportion of the third unheard from are unsuccessful, this is a record of usefulness.

questions.prompt: Du Bois calls the graduates “conservative, careful leaders” who “have seldom been agitators.” Why stress this, and what does the detail about Tuskegee prove?
facilitatorNotes: To reassure readers who feared that college would breed radicals. Tuskegee’s own teachers came largely from Fisk and Atlanta, down to “the energetic wife of the principal,” so Washington’s industrial school depends on the colleges it is said to replace. The reassurance sits a little oddly beside Du Bois’s own call, in Chapter III, for honest criticism of leaders.
evidence: They have seldom been agitators, have withstood the temptation to head the mob
almost from the beginning the backbone of Tuskegee's teaching force has been formed of graduates from Fisk and Atlanta

questions.prompt: “If white people need colleges to furnish teachers, ministers, lawyers, and doctors, do black people need nothing of the sort?” How does this question work as an argument?
facilitatorNotes: It argues from parity: a reader who says no must name a difference, and the only one available is the racial assumption Du Bois is attacking. “Who would do it if Negroes did not?” adds a practical point: in a segregated society Black communities need their own professionals. Some notice that the argument takes segregation as given.
evidence: Who would do it if Negroes did not?
do black people need nothing of the sort?

questions.prompt: Du Bois foresees the races living “side by side” yet “subtly and silently separate.” What will that require, and what irony does he find in the South’s “renaissance of university education”?
facilitatorNotes: “Social surgery” of the most delicate kind, needing broad-minded leaders of both races. The South is reviving universities for white students while the same voices that “cry hail” to it oppose higher education for Black students: it knows what culture is worth. Modern readers may be troubled that he accepts separation in “matters of deeper human intimacy” as part of the future.
evidence: it will call for social surgery at once the delicatest and nicest in modern history
But the very voices that cry hail to this good work are, strange to relate, largely silent or antagonistic to the higher education of the Negro.

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: “I sit with Shakespeare” (Chapter VI, end)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that ends by leaving argument for a vision.
readings.focus: The Talented Tenth, the counter-cries of the wronged, and the life of the mind above the Veil.
readings.context: Recap: Du Bois has shown that Black college graduates became teachers, ministers and doctors, and that the South welcomes university education for whites while opposing it for Black students. “The Talented Tenth” is his name for the educated leaders a people needs; “hewers of wood and drawers of water” (Joshua 9) are menial laborers. Rhine-gold is the cursed treasure of Wagner’s operas. Balzac and Dumas are French novelists (Dumas’s grandmother was an enslaved woman of Saint-Domingue); Aristotle and Marcus Aurelius are ancient philosophers. From Mount Pisgah Moses saw the Promised Land he would not enter; Philistines and Amalekites were Israel’s enemies.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The fourth paragraph speaks of the rape of Black women by white men, of “concubinage and prostitution,” of accusations against Black men, and of lynching, and uses the period term “mulattoes.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Of the Training of Black Men,” the last five paragraphs; opens “Strange to relate! for this is certain, no secure civilization can be built in the South…”; closes “…from this high Pisgah, between Philistine and Amalekite, we sight the Promised Land?”.

questions.prompt: “Strange to relate!” What danger does Du Bois say the South invites by “slamming the door of opportunity,” and what do his figures for graduates show?
facilitatorNotes: Leadership would pass from men “taught to think” to “untrained demagogues”: people who have “tasted of the Tree of Life” will not stop thinking. Graduates from Northern colleges rose from 22 to 43 to nearly 100, and from Southern Black colleges from 143 to 413 to over 500: a growing “thirst for training.” Some readers hear in the “turbulent proletariat” an appeal to white fear.
evidence: they have tasted of the Tree of Life
will you make them satisfied with their lot?

questions.prompt: Du Bois turns to “O Southern Gentlemen!” and gives the “counter-cries” of Black Americans. Choose two and show how each turns an accusation back on the accuser. Why does he voice them as “they” and not “I”?
facilitatorNotes: “Who brought us?” answers complaints about their presence; legal marriage against “systematic concubinage”; the rape of Black women, written on two million faces, against charges of assault; slavery as “the arch-crime” against claims of racial criminality. He then says he “will not say such arguments are wholly justified,” a careful distance that still lets them stand as what nearly every Black American feels. Students may read the distance as caution or as rhetorical force.
evidence: If you deplore their presence here, they ask, Who brought us?
they answer that slavery was the arch-crime, and lynching and lawlessness its twin abortion

questions.prompt: “It must develop men.” What does Du Bois mean by “that higher individualism” that must persist above “our modern socialism” and “the worship of the mass”?
facilitatorNotes: Beyond its social uses, the college must protect “the sovereign human soul” free to grow in its own way, against both mass movements and money (“our Rhine-gold”). Black experience, he adds, may give the world “new points of view.” The idea of a Talented Tenth has been criticised as elitist; students can weigh that charge against this paragraph.
evidence: And finally, beyond all this, it must develop men.
there must come a loftier respect for the sovereign human soul that seeks to know itself and the world about it

questions.prompt: How does “I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not” answer the whole chapter, and what is the force of the closing questions?
facilitatorNotes: In books the color line does not hold: the great dead come “with no scorn nor condescension,” and Du Bois dwells “above the Veil.” The questions turn on America: “knightly” is ironic, “the dull red hideousness of Georgia” is the life the South would impose, and Pisgah suggests a Promised Land seen but not yet entered. Some read the paragraph as a private escape that leaves the Veil standing below; others as proof of what education gives that no one can take away.
evidence: I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not.
Is this the life you grudge us, O knightly America?

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: into the Black Belt (Chapter VII, part 1)
readings.challenge: Track how history is laid over a landscape seen from a train.
readings.focus: Georgia as the centre of “the Negro problem,” and the Jim Crow car that carries Du Bois into the Black Belt.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Chapter VII describes a journey through Dougherty County in southwest Georgia, part of the Black Belt, the band of rich dark soil and old cotton plantations where Black people far outnumbered white. The epigraph is from the Song of Solomon in the Bible. Sam Hose, a Black farm laborer, was lynched by a mob in Georgia in 1899. James Oglethorpe founded the colony of Georgia, which at first banned slavery; George Whitefield was a famous preacher who pressed for allowing it. The revolution led by Toussaint Louverture in Haiti, from 1791, frightened slaveholders everywhere. A “Jim Crow car” was the railway car to which Black passengers were restricted.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage alludes to a lynching and describes segregated travel.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from the epigraph to the founding of the Cotton Kingdom; opens “I am black but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, As the tents of Kedar, as the…”; closes “…with the rich black swamp-land; and here the corner-stone of the Cotton Kingdom was laid.”.

questions.prompt: Why might Du Bois open a chapter on the Black Belt with these verses from the Song of Solomon?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker asserts her beauty against those who look down on her blackness, and says she was made to keep others’ vineyards while her own went untended. The chapter will show Black tenants working land owned by others. The epigraph claims dignity before the description begins.
evidence: Look not upon me, because I am black,
But mine own vineyard have I not kept.

questions.prompt: The land from the train is “bare and monotonous,” yet Du Bois says “this is historic ground.” What histories does he lay over it, and why does he call Sam Hose “crucified”?
facilitatorNotes: De Soto’s march and captives, the Cherokee and Creek lands taken, the colonial slave trade, the lynching of Sam Hose. The plain landscape becomes a record of conquest and violence. “Crucified” turns a lynching into a martyrdom and charges the mob with the crime of Christ’s killers.
evidence: for this is historic ground
not far from where Sam Hose was crucified

questions.prompt: What does Du Bois’s irony target in his account of colonial Georgia and the slave trade?
facilitatorNotes: The colonists “took the law into their own hands” to bring in slaves, “like some of their descendants,” a glance at lynch mobs. Pliant judges, smugglers and a preacher’s prayers all served the trade, which “went merrily on.” Law, courts and religion are shown giving way to profit.
evidence: these Georgians, like some of their descendants, proceeded to take the law into their own hands
the slave-trade went merrily on for fifty years and more

questions.prompt: “If you wish to ride with me you must come into the ‘Jim Crow Car.’” Who is the “you” Du Bois addresses, and what does the scene show about segregation?
facilitatorNotes: He addresses a white reader, who may sit in the Black car without objection, as four white men already do, while Du Bois may not enter the white coach. Segregation runs one way. The car is “fairly clean and comfortable”; the discomfort is humiliation, felt by the Black passengers and the author.
evidence: There will be no objection,--already four other white men, and a little white girl with her nurse, are in there.
The discomfort lies chiefly in the hearts of those four black men yonder--and in mine.

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: Albany and the Cotton Kingdom (Chapter VII, part 2)
readings.challenge: Watch how Du Bois corrects familiar pictures of Black country people.
readings.focus: A county town on market day, and the ruin of the great plantations.
readings.context: Recap: Du Bois has ridden the Jim Crow car south from Atlanta into the Black Belt of Georgia, recalling the region’s Indian removals, slave trade and cotton boom, and has reached Albany, seat of Dougherty County, with ten thousand Black and two thousand white inhabitants. The Rhine Palatinate (“Rhine-pfalz”), Naples and Cracow are European farming regions and cities Du Bois knew from his student years in Germany. A barony is a nobleman’s estate; whilom means former; rack-rent is an extortionate rent; “yellow” was a period term for a light-skinned Black person.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A white planter is remembered for killing Black people, and the slur used of them is quoted; land is said to have “passed to Jews and Negroes,” the first of the chapter’s generalisations about Jewish landowners.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from Albany on a Saturday to the owner of two hundred and forty acres; opens “Albany is to-day a wide-streeted, placid, Southern town, with a broad sweep of stores and…”; closes “…he is getting on, but cotton is down to four cents; I know how Debt sits staring at him.”.

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois describe the crowds that fill Albany on Saturday? What is the effect of his last words, “happy? well no, not exactly happy”?
facilitatorNotes: He compares them with peasants of the Rhineland, Naples and Cracow, placing them among the world’s country people rather than in an American caricature. The hesitating answer refuses the stereotype of the carefree Negro without denying their pleasure in the day.
evidence: far more silent and brooding than the crowds of the Rhine-pfalz, or Naples, or Cracow
happy? well no, not exactly happy, but much happier than as though they had not come

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois call Albany “a real capital,” and what does he ask the reader to imagine?
facilitatorNotes: It is the market, news-centre and court for ten thousand people spread over three hundred square miles: a city with its streets stretched into the countryside. Since modern readers know cities better than country life, he reverses the old comparison to make rural Black life visible.
evidence: Thus Albany is a real capital
we must imagine a little city of black people scattered far and wide over three hundred lonesome square miles of land

questions.prompt: What has happened to the great plantations of the Fields, Reasor and others? How does Du Bois explain the neglect of the land?
facilitatorNotes: The masters’ families are scattered, the land mortgaged or sold, and a distant heir or creditor collects “the rack-rent remorselessly” from Black tenants. The neglect is caused by the system of absentee ownership, not by the tenants, who stand it “only because they must.” Elegy (“the souls of them are passed”) and economic analysis sit side by side.
evidence: the souls of them are passed
Only black tenants can stand such a system, and they only because they must.

questions.prompt: “This, then, is the Cotton Kingdom … And where is the King?” How does Du Bois answer his own question, and how does the landowner with two hundred and forty acres complicate the answer?
facilitatorNotes: The “King” of the old saying “Cotton is King” may now be the ploughman fighting debt with two lean mules. Even the successful Black landowner, with tenants, a gin and children at school, is ruled by a falling price and by Debt, which Du Bois personifies as a watcher at his side.
evidence: Perhaps this is he,--the sweating ploughman, tilling his eighty acres with two lean mules
I know how Debt sits staring at him.

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: churches, fences and a silent plantation (Chapter VII, part 3)
readings.challenge: Find the economic explanation Du Bois gives for what looks like a matter of habit.
readings.focus: Churches and schools, fences, and a plantation ruined by dishonest Northern capital.
readings.context: Recap: Driving south from Albany through Dougherty County, Georgia, Du Bois has passed the remnants of great cotton plantations, worked now by Black tenants under heavy rents, and met a Black landowner struggling with debt and four-cent cotton. Lodges and burial societies were mutual-aid associations; Memnon was a Black king in Greek legend, famed for his beauty; “the Wizard of the North” is Du Bois’s fairy-tale name for Northern investors in the South after the war; curlews are long-legged wading birds.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Du Bois uses period color terms (“yellow man”) and speaks of “the Negro problem in its naked dirt and penury.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from the ruined home-houses to the end of the first day’s drive; opens “Wherever the King may be, the parks and palaces of the Cotton Kingdom have not wholly…”; closes “…field, white-turbaned and black-limbed. All this we saw, but the spell still lay upon us.”.

questions.prompt: What do Shepherd’s church and the little schoolhouse tell you about the community? Notice the humor.
facilitatorNotes: The church on stilts looks ready to “waddle off,” yet it is the centre of a hundred homes and draws five hundred people. The schoolhouse is “the cheerfulest” Du Bois has seen in the county outside town, though it holds rough benches and a broken stove: praise that measures how poor the others are. The flourishing burial societies show people providing for themselves.
evidence: looking for all the world as though it were just resting here a moment and might be expected to waddle off down the road
It is the cheerfulest schoolhouse I have seen in Dougherty, save in town.

questions.prompt: “I think I never before quite realized the place of the Fence in civilization.” What do fences mean to Du Bois, and why don’t tenants build them?
facilitatorNotes: A fence marks ownership, care and a stake in the future, and where he sees one he expects a prosperous home. Tenants on rack-rented land have every reason not to improve it: “It will only increase their rent.” What might look like shiftlessness is a rational answer to the terms of tenancy.
evidence: This is the Land of the Unfenced
why should they build fences on the rack-rented land? It will only increase their rent.

questions.prompt: Retell the tale of the Waters-Loring plantation. Who is the Wizard of the North, and what broke the spell?
facilitatorNotes: Northern capital came in the 1870s, bought a square mile, and for a while the gins and mills ran. Then the agents stole, and the company in anger let everything rot rather than sell. The ruin is caused by dishonesty and spite on the investors’ side, not by Black labor; it stands as a “rebuke.”
evidence: The Wizard of the North--the Capitalist--had rushed down in the seventies to woo this coy dark soil.
So the Waters-Loring plantation was stilled by the spell of dishonesty

questions.prompt: The drive back is described in lovely images. How does the last paragraph relate to what Du Bois saw that day?
facilitatorNotes: Pines, a pond, curlews and garnet cotton blooms make a painter’s scene, but “the spell still lay upon us”: the beauty cannot dispel the depression of ruin. The girl hoeing appears as a figure in a landscape; readers may ask whether the picturesque view keeps her at a distance.
evidence: the garnet blooms of the cotton looked gay against the green and purple stalks
A peasant girl was hoeing in the field, white-turbaned and black-limbed.
All this we saw, but the spell still lay upon us.

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: the Egypt of the Confederacy (Chapter VII)
readings.challenge: Hear the two meanings in a name.
readings.focus: The history of one Georgia county, from war with the Creeks to the richest slave kingdom and its fall.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). In Chapter VII Du Bois travels by carriage through Dougherty County, in the Black Belt of southwest Georgia, where Black tenants on old cotton plantations far outnumbered white people. Here he turns from the people he meets to the county’s past. Osceola led the Seminole resistance to removal from Florida in the 1830s, and Black people who had escaped slavery fought beside the Seminoles. Milan is famous for its great cathedral. In the Bible, Egypt is both the granary that fed its starving neighbors and the land where the Israelites were enslaved. The nouveau riche are the newly rich.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A formerly enslaved man’s testimony uses a racial slur and tells of people dying in the furrow and blood in the guard-house; Du Bois writes of chained convicts and calls the planters’ farming “the hard ruthless rape of the land.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from the swamp of the Chickasawhatchee to “the Egypt of the Confederacy”; opens “How curious a land is this,--how full of untold story, of tragedy and laughter, and the…”; closes “…is the Egypt of the Confederacy, and what meaning has it for the nation's weal or woe?”.

questions.prompt: Du Bois describes the swamp as beautiful and then remembers a war fought in it. How does the landscape carry its history? What does “Small wonder the wood is red” mean?
facilitatorNotes: The smouldering fire in “dull red anger” becomes blood remembered from the war of seventy years before. Even the road through the green “cathedral” was “built by chained Negro convicts.” Beauty and violence are inseparable in this ground.
evidence: In one place the wood is on fire, smouldering in dull red anger; but nobody minds.
a raised road, built by chained Negro convicts
Small wonder the wood is red.

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois build his picture of the slave kingdom of 1860? What two kinds of evidence does he combine?
facilitatorNotes: Sounds (the clank of chained feet, songs, wails, curses) and statistics (a hundred and fifty “barons,” six thousand enslaved people, ninety thousand acres, three million dollars). Feeling and figures together make the wealth and its cost concrete; the word “barons” makes the planters a feudal nobility.
evidence: Day after day the clank of chained feet marching from Virginia and Carolina to Georgia was heard in these rich swamp lands.
A hundred and fifty barons commanded the labor of nearly six thousand negroes

questions.prompt: “For was not all this show and tinsel built upon a groan?” Who answers Du Bois’s question, and why might Du Bois give him the last word on slavery?
facilitatorNotes: A ragged, grave-faced man by a blacksmith’s shop, who saw people “drop dead in the furrow” while “the plough never stopped.” Testimony from someone who lived it outweighs any description by an outsider, and his plain words cut through the romance of the “big house.”
evidence: built upon a groan
This land was a little Hell,
the plough never stopped

questions.prompt: Men called Dougherty “the Egypt of the Confederacy.” What two meanings can the name carry, and how does Du Bois use both?
facilitatorNotes: Egypt the granary: it fed the Confederate armies. Egypt the house of bondage: its wealth came from slavery. Du Bois adds that the cause was “lost long before 1861” and that the planters’ farming exhausted the soil. He ends by asking what the place now means for “the nation’s weal or woe.”
evidence: the rich granary whence potatoes and corn and cotton poured out to the famished and ragged Confederate troops
the hard ruthless rape of the land began to tell
what is the Egypt of the Confederacy, and what meaning has it for the nation's weal or woe?

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: debt and the convict farm (Chapter VII, part 4)
readings.challenge: Separate Du Bois’s analysis of a system from his generalisations about a group.
readings.focus: Debt, convict labor and two men’s answers to a life without reward.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). In Chapter VII Du Bois rides through Dougherty County, in the Black Belt of southwest Georgia. He has recalled its history as a rich slave kingdom, “the Egypt of the Confederacy,” ruined by war and by exhausting the soil. Under convict leasing, Southern states and counties rented prisoners, most of them Black, to planters and companies as forced labor; “the stockade” was the county prison. The colony of Georgia was promoted as a refuge for English debtors. A quadroon was a person with one Black grandparent; the Land of Canaan is the promised land of the Bible.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Du Bois generalises about Jewish landowners in antisemitic terms (“The Jew is the heir of the slave-baron”; “only a Yankee or a Jew could squeeze more blood”); he revised several of these remarks for the book’s 1953 edition. The passage mentions a Black youth hanged for rape, convict labor, a police killing and a man’s vow to kill any white man who strikes him.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from “a land of rapid contrasts” to Sears under the oak-trees; opens “It is a land of rapid contrasts and of curiously mingled hope and pain. Here sits a…”; closes “…of the Negro problem which we met that day, and we scarce knew which we preferred.”.

questions.prompt: What two accounts of the “stockade” does Du Bois report, and how does his description of the Bolton estate show which he believes? How might the “worthless black boy” who “was hanged for rape” bear on the question?
facilitatorNotes: White people say the prison is full of Black criminals; Black people say men are jailed because the State wants their forced labor. Writing in his own voice about the convict farm, Du Bois confirms the second: convict labor was “a way of making Negroes work,” and guilt was “a minor one.” The flat “so he was hanged” suggests a charge used as a pretext.
evidence: the black folks say that only colored boys are sent to jail, and they not because they are guilty, but because the State needs criminals to eke out its income by their forced labor
it was a way of making Negroes work, and the question of guilt was a minor one
so he was hanged for rape

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois show debt as a system rather than a personal failing? What does he mean by “a slave at twenty-two”?
facilitatorNotes: Debt runs in a chain from wholesaler to laborer; a tenant’s small crop goes in rent and in interest on supplies bought on credit; the soil yields an eighth of what it did. A young man who lost everything when cotton fell now rents a mule for half its price each year: bound by debt as surely as by law. The irony of Georgia as a refuge for debtors sharpens the point.
evidence: the merchants are in debt to the wholesalers, the planters are in debt to the merchants, the tenants owe the planters
Poor lad!--a slave at twenty-two.
Of this meagre yield the tenant pays from a quarter to a third in rent, and most of the rest in interest on food and supplies bought on credit.

questions.prompt: Du Bois writes that “The Jew is the heir of the slave-baron.” How does this generalisation sit beside his own evidence about who profits from the land?
facilitatorNotes: His evidence names many profiteers: a white New Englander, the state’s convict system, the master’s sons who seize Carter’s estate, the merchants and wholesalers. Singling out Jewish owners repeats a common stereotype of the Jewish creditor and blames a group for a system he elsewhere analyses. It is a hard case: a writer exposing racial generalisation uses one himself, and later revised the lines.
evidence: The Jew is the heir of the slave-baron in Dougherty
only a Yankee or a Jew could squeeze more blood from debt-cursed tenants
And them white folks will get it, too,

questions.prompt: The red-eyed man and Sears react to the same conditions in opposite ways. Why does Du Bois end by saying “we scarce knew which we preferred”?
facilitatorNotes: One, embittered after forty-five years and the news of a police killing, vows violence; the other laughs, flips pebbles and keeps his children from school. Du Bois romanticises neither: “Careless ignorance and laziness here, fierce hate and vindictiveness there.” Both are products of the system, and the honest uncertainty leaves the reader with the problem.
evidence: Let a white man touch me, and he dies
we scarce knew which we preferred

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: a faded “Welcome” (Chapter VII, end)
readings.challenge: Collect the obstacles in a series of brief portraits.
readings.focus: Ruined houses, Black farmers who rose, and the ways their efforts were blocked.
readings.context: Recap: Riding through southwest Dougherty County, Georgia, Du Bois has met Black tenants trapped in debt, seen the old Bolton convict farm, and heard one man who had worked forty-five years for nothing swear to kill any white man who touched him. A factor is a business agent; “the revolution of ’63” is Du Bois’s shorthand for the war and emancipation; the Cotton Seed Oil Trust was a combination of companies controlling the cottonseed business; Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Household furniture was protected by law from seizure for debt.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. An old man’s speech, as Du Bois reports it, uses a racial slur; a young man kills his baby and his wife and then himself; Du Bois again generalises about Jewish landowners.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Of the Black Belt,” from the old man who cleared his own land to the end of the chapter; opens “Here and there we meet distinct characters quite out of the ordinary. One came out of a…”; closes “…exempt from seizure by law." "Well, he took it just the same," said the hard-faced man.”.

questions.prompt: What puzzles Du Bois about the old man who cleared his own piece of woods? How does the man handle his visitors?
facilitatorNotes: His deep bows have an “imperturbable gravity that seemed almost suspicious,” as if he were performing deference; his “Oh, I gets along with white folks” is said “eyeing us.” He gives away little and watches them go without seeming to notice them. Readers may connect this guarded performance with the “double-consciousness” of the book’s first chapter.
evidence: with an imperturbable gravity that seemed almost suspicious
Oh, I gets along with white folks.
looking after us, and yet apparently not noticing us

questions.prompt: Du Bois gives sympathy to the ruined white families too. What does the story of the “sad-colored house” show, and how is it told?
facilitatorNotes: The war and emancipation overturned fortunes, and the masters’ sons inherited poverty and bitterness. The murder of a wife and baby and the son’s suicide are told in one flat sentence, then “And the world passed on”: the brevity makes the indifference felt. The chapter mourns ruin on both sides of the color line without excusing slavery.
evidence: A revolution such as that of '63 is a terrible thing; they that rose rich in the morning often slept in paupers' beds.
And the world passed on.

questions.prompt: Why might Du Bois stop at the empty house with the faded “Welcome” on its wall? What does the image sum up?
facilitatorNotes: The great house of Southern hospitality is a ruin, and its greeting now welcomes no one, least of all a Black traveler peering through the broken door. The single faded word holds the whole decline of the Cotton Kingdom.
evidence: written in once gay letters a faded

questions.prompt: Sanford, Corliss, Jack Delson, the preacher’s wife, the hard-faced man: which of them prosper, and what blocks the others? What does the chapter’s last line say about the law?
facilitatorNotes: Delson owns six hundred and fifty acres, but Sanford cannot buy land the owner will not sell, Corliss is squeezed by a trust, the preacher’s family was cheated of land they paid for, and a sheriff seized furniture the law exempted. “He took it just the same”: the law gives no protection to people who cannot enforce it.
evidence: but the owner will not sell off a few acres
the Cotton Seed Oil Trust has forced the price of ginning so low that he says it hardly pays him
but they cheated us out of it
Well, he took it just the same,

readings.title: The Souls of Black Folk: the golden fleece (Chapter VIII)
readings.challenge: Follow Du Bois from myth to statistics and ask what each kind of writing does for his argument.
readings.focus: Cotton as the modern Golden Fleece, and why the Black Belt deserves honest study.
readings.context: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), historian and sociologist, was teaching at Atlanta University when he gathered these essays on Black American life after Emancipation as The Souls of Black Folk (1903). In Chapter VII Du Bois rode through Dougherty County, a cotton county in the Black Belt of southwest Georgia; Chapter VIII studies its Black farm laborers closely. In Greek myth Jason and his Argonauts sailed to the Black Sea for the Golden Fleece of a winged ram; to win it Jason sowed dragon’s teeth, which sprang up as armed men. The epigraph is from William Vaughn Moody’s poem “The Brute” (1901), in which the Brute stands for the machines of modern industry. The New South was the industrialising South after Reconstruction; a parvenu is an upstart newcomer.
readings.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement; its historical racial terminology and generalisations belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Of the Quest of the Golden Fleece,” from the epigraph to the cabins of Dougherty County; opens “But the Brute said in his breast, "Till the mills I grind have ceased, The riches shall…”; closes “…rooms; only fourteen have five rooms or more. The mass live in one- and two-room homes.”.

questions.prompt: What is the “golden fleece” of the title, and where is it now “woven”? What does the comparison with Jason’s quest suggest about the wealth of cotton?
